clinicalPearls: Caused by variants in SCN8A, which encodes the voltage-gated sodium channel alpha subunit Nav1.6, a channel highly expressed at the axon initial segment and nodes of Ranvier

Most classic developmental and epileptic encephalopathy cases arise from gain-of-function variants that increase neuronal excitability, and these children often respond preferentially to sodium-channel-blocking antiseizure agents
Seizure onset is usually in infancy, with focal, tonic, and epileptic-spasm semiologies and frequent progression to intractable mixed seizure types
Development is typically impaired, ranging from mild delay to profound intellectual disability with movement disorder, hypotonia evolving to spasticity, and cortical visual impairment
A milder end of the spectrum includes benign familial infantile epilepsy that remits, while a separate phenotype presents with intellectual disability and movement disorder without prominent seizures
Loss-of-function SCN8A variants tend to cause a distinct milder phenotype and, in contrast to gain-of-function disease, sodium-channel blockers may be unhelpful or aggravating
There is a recognised risk of sudden unexpected death in epilepsy, reinforcing the importance of seizure control and family counselling
reference.pathophysiology: SCN8A encodes Nav1.6, a voltage-gated sodium channel concentrated at the axon initial segment and nodes of Ranvier where it drives action potential initiation and repetitive firing. Gain-of-function variants shift channel gating so that neurons become hyperexcitable, for example through impaired inactivation or a persistent inward sodium current, producing early severe epilepsy and encephalopathy. Loss-of-function variants reduce channel availability and are generally associated with milder phenotypes without early catastrophic seizures. Because the therapeutic response depends on the functional consequence of the variant, distinguishing gain from loss of function guides rational selection of antiseizure medication.
additionalDifferentials: Other early infantile epileptic encephalopathies of genetic cause
Structural or metabolic epilepsies of infancy
additionalInvestigations: Epilepsy gene panel or trio whole-exome sequencing to identify the SCN8A variant and infer likely functional effect
Prolonged or video electroencephalography to characterise seizure types and interictal abnormalities
Brain magnetic resonance imaging, often normal early but useful to exclude structural causes
Functional or in silico assessment of the variant where available to distinguish gain from loss of function
Developmental and neuropsychological assessment to document trajectory
Electrocardiography and cardiac review given sodium-channel expression and SUDEP considerations
redFlags: Clusters of intractable seizures or evolving status epilepticus in infancy
Developmental regression or plateau accompanying seizure onset
Emerging movement disorder or profound hypotonia with feeding and respiratory compromise
Features suggesting heightened sudden unexpected death in epilepsy risk
reference.prognosis: Outcome varies widely by variant: gain-of-function developmental and epileptic encephalopathy often carries drug-resistant seizures, significant intellectual disability, and a raised risk of sudden unexpected death, whereas milder self-limited or predominantly movement-disorder phenotypes may have better cognitive outcomes.
pitfalls: Assuming all SCN8A disease is gain-of-function and reflexively using sodium-channel blockers, which can worsen loss-of-function cases
Overlooking the milder self-limited familial infantile epilepsy phenotype and over-treating
Attributing a normal early MRI to a benign course despite a severe genetic epilepsy
Neglecting counselling about sudden unexpected death in epilepsy and safety planning
references: GeneReviews: SCN8A-Related Epilepsy and/or Neurodevelopmental Disorders
ILAE classification and genetics resources on developmental and epileptic encephalopathies
management: Treat gain-of-function encephalopathy with sodium-channel-blocking antiseizure agents such as phenytoin, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, or lacosamide, which are preferentially effective
Reconsider or avoid sodium-channel blockers in loss-of-function variants, where they may be unhelpful or aggravating
Manage frequently drug-resistant mixed seizures with combination therapy and consideration of the ketogenic diet
Address the associated movement disorder, evolving hypotonia and spasticity, and cortical visual impairment with rehabilitation and supportive therapies
Provide cardiac assessment and counsel on the raised risk of sudden unexpected death in epilepsy
Undertake developmental and neuropsychological surveillance with early intervention
Offer genetic counselling and refer to paediatric neurology and epileptology
